newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FOCUS - Pakistan's president, military expand powers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pakistan's president, military expand powers.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari's bold creation of a national security council, with elections just four weeks away, tilts power towards the presidency and the military, analysts said on Tuesday.
Reaction from most political parties has been hostile, although mixed opinions came from Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML), widely tipped to top the polls set for February 3.
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index shed 17.37 points to close at 1,338.66 as investors responded cautiously to a move that some brokers said could aggravate political uncertainty.

Leghari launched his far-reaching initiative with the approval of a caretaker cabinet that he named after dissolving the National Assembly and sacking Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule,
"It's a dramatic shift of power from the prime minister to the president and gives the army its first formal role in government affairs," a European diplomat said.

The 10-member Council for Defence and National Security, set up by a presidential order on Monday, includes the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff committee and the army, navy and air force chiefs, as well as the prime minister and the ministers for defence, foreign affairs, interior and finance.

The president, supreme commander of the armed forces, will chair the council, which is empowered to advise on defence and national security issues and on economic and financial policies affecting them. It can also make recommendations on internal security matters and the proclamation of an emergency.
The president may refer any issue to the council without consulting the prime minister in a potentially significant accretion of presidential power at the premier's expense.
In theory, the council's advice is not binding, but given the already powerful influence of the military in Pakistani politics, it would seem hard for a prime minister to defy it.
The caretaker government has sought to allay fears that the council's creation would subvert other organs of state.

"It is no supra-constitution, no supra-cabinet and no supra-government body," Information Minister Irshad Ahmad Haqqani said on Monday. He denied that the military had asked for the council or was seeking to share power with civilians.

Aitzaz Ahsan, a leader of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, said Leghari was isolated and wanted the armed forces to support the economic policies of the interim cabinet, which he said had made Pakistan hostage to international lending agencies.
"Now they want the armed forces to share the responsibility for their misconceived policies," he told Dawn newspaper.
Cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan said it was for parliament to decide whether to set up permanent institutions.
Qazi Hussain Ahmed, chief of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party, said Leghari had overstepped his constitutional powers.
Sartaj Aziz, secretary general of the PML, said the move could create "some public concern that such a body might adversely affect the evolution of a parliamentary system".

But PML Information Secretary Mushahid Hussain told The News daily that his party felt the security council was necessary. "It should promote economic development and national cohesion...so that the political forces and the armed forces could steer the country out of crises," he said.

Leghari and Shahid Javed Burki, the prime minister's adviser on finance and economic affairs, have repeatedly stressed the need for an incoming elected government to uphold pledges made by the caretakers to the International Monetary Fund.
The president has said he will personally try to ensure that stabilisation measures and economic reforms launched during the three-month interim are not abandoned later.
Some Karachi brokers said the security council could play a valuable role in ensuring continuity and good governance.
"There is no harm in including the military in government affairs as everyone knows that they are already involved," said Anisur Rehman, head of research at Crosby Securities.
Stocks analysts said the change was unlikely to cheer the market, hit by a liquidity crunch and lack of foreign interest, as well as worries about the elections and next year's budget.

Some analysts saw Leghari's move as part of a deal whereby the army would let the elections go ahead and the PML take power under constraints imposed by the military, while the president would serve out the remaining two years of his five-year term.
"If this is the case, it is a worryingly short-term basis for such a major change," the European diplomat said.
